'Come down. Ten minutes on the platform, then back.' They walked the length of the train and stretched their arms over their heads, laughing at a monkey on the roof. passage: Clara, ten, noticed it on Gabriel's first week at the school in Seville. The new boy used a wheelchair, and at break the others stood in a tight group, staring and whispering. One asked loudly, 'What happened to your legs?' Gabriel went red. Then nobody asked him to play tag. Clara felt uncomfortable, but she didn't know what to do. The next day their teacher, Señora Ruiz, sat with the class. 'It's fine to be curious. Gabriel, would you like to tell us about your chair, or which games you like?' Gabriel shrugged, then grinned. 'I'm really fast on the basketball court.' That break Clara went up to him. 'Want to be on my team?' They lost, but Gabriel scored twice, and the group stopped whispering.

qa.q: What game did Gabriel say he was fast at?
qa.a: Basketball.

qa.q: What was Clara feeling during Gabriel's first week?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and unsure, seeing him stared at and left out but not knowing what to do.

qa.q: What did Señora Ruiz model for the class?
qa.a: Respectful curiosity: asking Gabriel if he wanted to share, and finding games he enjoys, instead of staring or blunt questions.

qa.q: How might Gabriel have felt when asked 'What happened to your legs?'
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and singled out, going red in front of everyone.

grounding: Shows a child noticing classmates staring at and excluding a disabled peer, and a teacher modelling respectful curiosity and inclusion.

subtype: Classmates curious or careless [Observer]
passage: In the Class 4 art room, Usha Ma'am heard the whisper behind her. 'Why does Wasim have that thing in his ear? Is he deaf?' Two boys giggled. Wasim, nine, lowered his head and pretended to colour. Usha felt a flash of anger, then took a breath. She didn't scold the boys in front of everyone. She sat at their table. 'Good question, but let's ask kindly. Wasim, would you like to tell us about your hearing aid, or would you rather not?' Wasim hesitated, then held it up. 'It makes sounds louder. I can hear you better with it.' 'That's clever,' said one boy. Usha nodded. 'Different bodies need different tools.' At the end of the lesson she asked Wasim to hand out the paints, and the boys chatted with him as he did.

qa.q: What did Wasim do when the boys giggled?
qa.a: He lowered his head and pretended to colour.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she heard the whisper?
qa.a: She felt a flash of anger, then calmed herself before responding.

qa.q: Why did Usha give Wasim the choice to share or not?
qa.a: It respected his privacy and dignity while showing the class how to ask kindly.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt holding up his hearing aid?
qa.a: He was probably nervous at first, then relieved when the boy said it was clever.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing children's blunt questions about a disabled peer and modelling respectful curiosity and inclusion.

subtype: Classmates curious or careless [Observer]
passage: I'm Kiran, and I was in Pallavi's class the year she came back after her operation. She walked with crutches, slowly. At lunch, a few girls said she'd slow them down in hopscotch, and they just started without her. Pallavi sat on the step, watching, pretending she didn't mind. I don't know exactly what she was feeling. But she didn't eat her lunch. The next day our class teacher, Mr Dsilva, asked us all to invent a new game where everyone could play, sitting or standing. Pallavi came up with one using a ball and chalk circles. We played it all term. I remember thinking I should have done something myself, the first day. I didn't. I'm still a bit ashamed about that.

qa.q: What did Pallavi use to walk?
qa.a: Crutches.

qa.q: What does Kiran feel looking back on the first day?
qa.a: Kiran feels a bit ashamed about not doing something to include Pallavi.

qa.q: What did Mr Dsilva do to model inclusion?
qa.a: He asked the class to invent a game everyone could play, which let Pallavi join and lead.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt sitting on the step?
qa.a: She probably felt left out and hurt, even though she pretended not to mind.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's account, children leaving out a disabled peer and a teacher modelling inclusion so that difference is not seen as a flaw.

subtype: Missing school and friends because of illness [Actor]
passage: Every other week, Aadhya, ten, travelled with her father on the bus from their village to the district hospital for her kidney treatment. Each trip meant three days away from school. She missed the Republic Day practice and Maya's birthday, and when she came back, the class was on a new chapter and the girls had new jokes she didn't understand. She sat alone at lunch, feeling like a visitor. Parveen Ma'am noticed. She started sending a notebook home with Aadhya's neighbour, with simple notes on each missed lesson. She asked two classmates to write letters too. On Aadhya's next hospital trip, she opened the notebook on the bus and found a drawing from Maya: 'Come back soon, we saved your seat.' Aadhya smiled for the whole journey.

qa.q: What did Maya write on the drawing?
qa.a: 'Come back soon, we saved your seat.'

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when she came back to school?
qa.a: She felt lonely and left behind, like a visitor who did not understand the new jokes.

qa.q: What did Parveen Ma'am do to keep Aadhya connected?
qa.a: She sent notes on missed lessons and asked classmates to write letters.

qa.q: How might Maya have felt when Aadhya missed her birthday?
qa.a: Maya may have felt a little sad, and the drawing shows she wanted Aadhya to feel missed.

grounding: Shows a child whose frequent hospital trips make her miss lessons and friends and feel lonely, and a teacher and classmates keeping her connected.

subtype: Missing school and friends because of illness [Actor]
passage: Astrid, nine, spent more of the autumn in the Stockholm children's hospital than at school. Her blood condition meant treatments that left her tired and away for weeks at a time. She missed the class trip to the forest and felt the others were growing up without her. One evening, her phone buzzed: a video call from her best friend Lucia. 'Look!' Lucia held up a jar of pine cones. 'We saved you the best ones from the trip.' Their teacher had also started sending short, easier versions of the maths homework, so Astrid could keep up in small bits. Every Friday the class did a five-minute call with her, waving and shouting news. Astrid still felt lonely some days. But on Fridays she felt like she belonged.

qa.q: What did Lucia save from the trip?
qa.a: A jar of pine cones.

qa.q: How did Astrid feel about missing school?
qa.a: She felt lonely and left behind, as if the others were growing up without her.

qa.q: What did the teacher and Lucia do that helped?
qa.a: They kept in touch with calls and saved things from the trip, and the teacher adapted the homework into small parts.

qa.q: How might Lucia feel on the Friday calls?
qa.a: Lucia is probably happy to see her friend and glad to share news with her.

grounding: Shows a child whose hospital stays make her miss lessons and friends and feel lonely, and friends and a teacher who keep in touch and adapt work.

subtype: Missing school and friends because of illness [Actor]
passage: On the children's ward of the Pune hospital, Zeenat, eleven, sat in the small hospital schoolroom with a drip in her arm. It was her third stay this term. 'My class is doing a science fair,' she told the ward teacher, Binita Ma'am. 'I'll miss it again.' Her voice went flat. Binita pulled up a chair. 'What if we call your class teacher and find out if you can still take part?' That afternoon they spoke on the phone. Zeenat's teacher said she could send in a project, and her group would present it for her. Binita helped her grow cress seeds on damp cotton on the windowsill. A week later, her group sent a photo from the fair: her cress, labelled 'By Zeenat, from Ward 3'. Zeenat pinned it above her bed.

qa.q: What did Zeenat grow on the windowsill?
qa.a: Cress seeds on damp cotton.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel about missing the science fair?
qa.a: She felt left out and down, her voice going flat.

qa.q: What did Binita Ma'am do to keep Zeenat connected?
qa.a: She called Zeenat's class teacher, arranged for her to send a project, and helped her grow it on the ward.

qa.q: How might Zeenat's group feel presenting her project?
qa.a: They probably felt proud and glad to include her even though she was in hospital.

grounding: Shows a child whose hospital stays make her miss school events and feel lonely, and teachers who keep in touch and adapt so she stays connected.

subtype: Wanting to be treated as normal [Actor]
passage: Tuan, fifteen, had asthma, but nobody on his Oslo football team knew. He hid his inhaler in his jacket and skipped it before matches, because he hated the thought of anyone seeing. During a hard game in the cold, his chest went tight and he had to stop, bent over and wheezing. His coach, Ulla, jogged over. She didn't make a fuss. 'Where's your inhaler?' He pointed. She brought the jacket, then stood so the others couldn't see. Afterwards she sat with him. 'You don't have to tell the team anything. But I need you safe. What would make it easier for you?' Tuan thought. 'If I could use it in the changing room before, without questions.' 'Deal. Your choice who knows.' He nodded, relieved.

qa.q: Where did Tuan hide his inhaler?
qa.a: In his jacket.

qa.q: Why did Tuan skip his inhaler before matches?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and afraid of standing out if anyone saw him use it.

qa.q: What made Ulla's approach work?
qa.a: She respected Tuan's privacy, asked what would make it easier and let him choose, while making his safety clear.

qa.q: How might Tuan's teammates have reacted if Ulla had announced his asthma?
qa.a: They might have stared or treated him differently, which is exactly what Tuan feared.

grounding: Shows a teenager hiding symptoms and skipping treatment to avoid standing out, and a coach whose support respects his choice and dignity.

subtype: Wanting to be treated as normal [Actor]
passage: In the school nurse's room, Preeti, sixteen, sat with her arms crossed. She had type 1 diabetes and had stopped doing her lunchtime blood checks because her friends stared when she used the kit in the canteen. That morning she'd felt shaky in chemistry. Devika Ma'am, the nurse, didn't lecture. 'You're sixteen. You know your body better than I do. What's getting in the way?' Preeti stared at the floor. 'Everyone watches. I just want to be normal.' Devika nodded. 'That makes sense. What if you did your checks here, in private, whenever you like? No one needs to know unless you tell them.' Preeti looked up. 'Really?' 'Your plan, your choice. I'm just here if you need me.' The next day Preeti came in at lunch, on her own.

qa.q: Where did Preeti stop doing her blood checks?
qa.a: In the canteen.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling about the blood checks?
qa.a: She felt self-conscious and embarrassed, wanting to be normal and not watched.

qa.q: What did Devika Ma'am do that respected Preeti's independence?
qa.a: She asked what was in the way and offered a private space, letting Preeti make the plan.

qa.q: How might Preeti's friends have seen the kit in the canteen?
qa.a: They may have been simply curious, not realising how watched and different their staring made Preeti feel.

grounding: Shows a teenager skipping treatment to avoid standing out, and support that respects her choice and dignity working better than control.

subtype: Wanting to be treated as normal [Actor]
passage:
Dear Coach Francis,
I'm writing because I can't say this properly at practice. Since you found out about my condition, you've benched me every time I look tired, and you ask me in front of everyone if I've taken my tablets. I know you mean well. But it makes me feel like a patient, not a player. Last month I even stopped mentioning when I felt dizzy, because I didn't want to be benched. That was stupid, I know.
Here's what I'd like instead. I take my tablets every morning. If I feel unwell, I'll tell you quietly and sit out. You don't need to ask in front of the team. My doctor says I can play.
Can we try it for a month?
Tushar

qa.q: When does Tushar take the tablets?
qa.a: Every morning.

qa.q: How does Tushar feel when asked about tablets in front of everyone?
qa.a: Tushar feels embarrassed and treated like a patient, not a player.

qa.q: What plan does Tushar propose?
qa.a: Tushar will take the tablets every morning and quietly tell the coach and sit out when unwell, without public questions.

qa.q: How might Coach Francis feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Coach Francis may feel surprised and a little hurt, but also relieved that Tushar wants to be honest about feeling unwell.

grounding: Shows a teenager who hid symptoms to avoid being singled out, asking for support that respects independence and dignity rather than control.
